items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the civil practice law and rules and the civil rights law, in relation to the right to privacy and persona rights
items.lawCode: Amd §215, CPLR; amd Art 5 Head & §§50 & 51, Civ Rts L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5857

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the civil practice law and rules and
the civil rights law, in relation to the right to privacy and persona
rights

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :

To add persona rights to Section 50 of the Civil Rights Law, Right of
Privacy.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 50(1) of the Civil Rights Law would be amended to define
"person" and "persona."

Section 50(2) would provide that a person who uses the persona of a
living or deceased person without written consent for advertising
and/or trade purposes would be guilty of a misdemeanor.

Section 50(3) would provide that, regarding a deceased person's
persona, the required written consent would be exercisable by the
person or persons who collectively own more than 50% of the rights of
the persona.

Section 50(4) would provide that this property right would exist in a
deceased individual who died on or after or within seventy years
before the effective date of this subdivision. It would further
provide that these property rights would be freely transferrable or
descendible, and would exist for seventy years after the death of the
individual.

Section 50(5) would provide that, in the absence of a transfer in a
testamentary instrument, a provision in a testamentary instrument that
provides for the disposition of the rest of a deceased person's assets
would be effective to transfer the individual's persona.

Section 50(6) would provide that persona rights recognized by a person
identified as entitled to inherit a deceased individual's property
under intestacy would not be affected.

Section 51(1) would provide an equitable cause of action for a
violation of this; a plaintiff could seek to prevent and restrain the
use of a persona, and/or damages.

Section 51(2) would require that such an action be brought within
three years of the date of discovery, or from the date through the
exercise of reasonable diligence such should have been discovered.

 JUSTIFICATION :

This bill would establish a property right in an individual's persona,
and would further establish that use of an individual's persona
without written consent for advertising and/or trade purposes would be
a misdemeanor. Such unauthorized use would also create a cause of
action; a plaintiff could seek to prevent and restrain the use of a
persona, and/or damages.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5857A

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the civil rights law, in relation to
the right of publicity; and to amend the civil practice law and rules,
in relation to the timeliness of commencement of an action for
violation of the right of publicity

 PURPOSE OF BILL :

To create a right of publicity for deceased individuals and a registry
to publicly post such interests upon thereby giving notice to people
who may seek to use an individual's right of publicity in New York
State for advertising purposes, or for the purposes of trade or for
purposes of fund-raising or solicitation of donations.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

§ .50. Definitions. For the purposes of sections fifty-f, fifty-g,
fifty-h, fifty-i and fifty one of this article, the following terms
are defined:

1. "Characteristic"

2. "Deceased individual"

3. "Secretary"

4. "Fund-raising"

5. "Individual"

6. "Likeness"

7. "Name"

8. "Person"

9. "Photograph"

10. "Registration to establish a claim of right"

11. "Right of publicity"

12. "Signature"

§ 50-f. Right of publicity for living and deceased individuals.
Creates a right of publicity for all individuals, whether living or
deceased, wherever they might be domiciled, for actions that occur
within New York State. This legislation establishes that a living or
deceased individual's name, voice, signature and likeness,
individually and collectively known as his or her right of publicity,
is personal property, freely transferable or descendible, in whole or
in part, by contract or by means of any trust or testamentary
instrument, whether such contract, trust or testamentary instrument
was entered into or executed before or after the effective date. An
individual's right of publicity cannot be used without obtaining the
written consent of the individual, his or her successors or assigns,
or in the case of a minor, of his or her parent or guardian.

§ 50-g. Duration of an individual's right of publicity. Establishes
that every individual's right of publicity continues to exist for
forty years after their death, and does not expire upon the death of
the individual, regardless of whether the law of the domicile,
residence, or citizenship of the individual at the time of death or
otherwise recognizes a similar or identical property right.

§ 50-h. Methods of transfer and conveyance. Establishes the ways that
an individual's right of publicity may be transferred, including by
contract, license, gift, trust, will, testamentary instrument or
intestacy. After an individual dies, the person who is his or her
successor in interest with an ownership of fifty one percent or more
of the decedent's right of publicity may register such interest with
the New York State secretary of state for a fee of $50.00. Unless the
right of publicity is registered and publicly posted by the secretary
of state on the public website maintained for that purpose, there is
no protection against the use of a deceased individual's right of
publicity. After forty years have passed, the deceased individual's
right of publicity is no longer protected against use in commerce and
trade. After forty seven years have passed the secretary of state may
destroy all information related to the lapsed right of publicity.

§ 50-i. No abrogation of rights and remedies. States that nothing
contained in the provisions of this article related to the right of
publicity shall be deemed to abrogate or otherwise limit any rights or
remedies otherwise conferred by federal or state law.

§ 51. Action for injunction and for damages. Subparagraph one
determines that this legislation applies to any act that occurs in New
York State regardless of the deceased individual's domicile,
residence, or citizenship. Subparagraph two discusses when consent for
use of another individual's right of publicity as provided in the
provisions of this Article pertaining to the right of publicity shall
not be required with a limited exception. The limited exception is in
response to the development and use of technology that allows a
variety of media forms to reproduce the right of publicity of
individuals, both living and dead, in a variety of contexts such as
movies, videogames and books on CD. Therefore, the statute provides
protections to the use of the life time and post mortem use of an
individual's right of publicity in the light of such technological
developments. Subparagraph three discusses limited immunities for
certain people unless it is established that the owners or employees
had knowledge of the unauthorized use. Subparagraph four states that
if an individual's right of publicity is used within this state for
advertising purposes, or for the purposes of trade or for purposes of
fund-raising or solicitation of donations, without the written consent
the individual is entitled to maintain an equitable action for
violation of the individual's right of publicity. In addition, to
prevent and restrain the use thereof; an individual may also sue and
recover damages for any injuries sustained, including an amount equal
to the greater of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or compensatory
damages by reason of such use and if the defendant shall have
knowingly used such person's right of publicity the finder of fact, in
its discretion, may award exemplary damages. Furthermore, a violation
of an individual's right of publicity may occur without regard to
whether the use or activity is for profit or not for profit.

 JUSTIFICATION :

The term "Right of Publicity" originated in the United States Court of
Appeals for the Second Circuit in 1953 in Haelan Laboratories v.
Topps Chewing Gum to describe the right of individuals to control the
use of their name and likenesses for commercial and other valuable
purposes. Since then, more than half of the states have granted rights
of publicity to individuals through either the common law or by
statute.

The Right of Publicity refers to every individual's inherent right to
control the commercial use of his or her personal characteristics,
which can include name, voice, signature, photograph, image, likeness,
distinctive appearance, gestures, or mannerisms. The most critical
function of the Right of Publicity is control. The Right of Publicity,
even though it is a property right, is not merely a property asset,
like a painting or real estate, for estate tax purposes. The Right of
Publicity ensures that if a person, or that person's successor in
interest, does not seek to commercialize the right, they are not
compelled to do so.

This bill provides for a post mortem right of publicity for forty
years after the death of an individual, allowing successors in
interest to provide notice of such interest through a public
registration and posting maintained by the New York Secretary of
State. Along with providing for a post mortem right of publicity the
bill also has exclusions consistent with constitutionally protected
freedom of speech.

Finally, the Right of Publicity created through this legislation
applies to acts that occur within New York State regardless of the
deceased individual's domicile, residence, or citizenship. This way we
are able to prevent anomalous results in the application of the law to
individuals who do not have a Right of Publicity in their domicile or
country.

In conclusion, this bill is balanced in protecting essential first
amendment rights consistent with current law while still providing
protections for an individual's right of publicity during life and for
forty years after death.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :

To be determined.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the one hundred eightieth day after it
shall have become a law, and shall apply to deceased individuals who
died on or after such date.

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5857B

SPONSOR: SAVINO
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the civil rights law, in relation to the right of priva-
cy and the right of publicity; and to amend the civil practice law and
rules, in relation to the timeliness of commencement of an action for
violation of the right of publicity

 
PURPOSE OF BILL:

To create a right of publicity for deceased individuals and a registry
to publicly post such interests upon thereby giving notice to people who
may seek to use an individual's right of publicity in New York State for
advertising purposes, or for the purposes of trade. In addition this
bill addresses the ability of technology to create digital avatars and
makes regulations regarding their use.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

§ .50. Definitions. For the purposes of sections fifty-f, fifty-g,
fifty-h, fifty-i and fifty one of this article, the following terms are
defined:

1. "Deceased individual"

2. "Digital replica"

3. "Secretary"

4. "Fund-raising"

5. "Individual"

6. "Name"

7. "Person"

8. "Persona"

9. "Right of privacy"

10. "Right of publicity"

11. "Signature"

§ 50-f. Right of publicity for living and deceased individuals.  Creates
a right of publicity for individuals, whether living or deceased, for
actions that occur within New York State. This legislation establishes
that a living or deceased individual's persona, is personal property,
freely transferable or descendible, in whole or in part, by contract or
by means of any trust or testamentary instrument, whether such contract,
trust or testamentary instrument was entered into or executed before or
after the effective date. An individual's right of publicity cannot be
used for advertising purposes or purposes of trade without obtaining the
written consent of the individual, his or her successors or assigns, or
in the case of a minor, of his or her parent or guardian as limited by

section 35.03 of the Arts and Cultural Affairs Law. Furthermore, a
parent may not assign a child's Right of Publicity.

§ 50-g. Duration of an individual's right of publicity. Establishes that
an individual's right of publicity continues to exist for forty years
after their death.

§ 50-h. Methods of transfer and conveyance. Establishes the ways that an
individual's right of publicity may be transferred, including by
contract, license, gift, trust, will, testamentary. instrument or intes-
tacy. After an individual dies, the person who is his or her successor
in interest with an ownership of fifty one percent or more of the
decedent's right of publicity may register such interest with the New
York State secretary of state for a fee of $100.00. Unless the right of
publicity is registered within six months of the individual's death
there is no protection against the use of a deceased individual's right
of publicity. After forty years have passed, the deceased individual's
right of publicity is no longer protected against use in advertising and
trade. After forty seven years have passed the secretary of state may
destroy all information related to the lapsed right of publicity.

§ 50-i. No abrogation of rights and remedies. States that nothing
contained in the provisions of this article related to the right of
publicity shall be deemed to abrogate or otherwise limit any rights or
remedies otherwise conferred by federal or state law.

§ 51. Action for injunction and for damages. Subparagraph one determines
that this legislation applies to any act that occurs in New York State.
Subparagraph two discusses when consent for use of another individual's
right of publicity as provided in the provisions of this Article
pertaining to the right of publicity shall not be required with a few
limited exception.

Subparagraph three discusses the use of digital replicas for purposes of
trade in an expressive work and limited immunities for such use.
Subparagraph four discusses the use of digital replicas in pornographic
work without the consent of the individual.  Subparagraph five discusses
the limited immunity for certain people unless it is established that
the owners or employees had knowledge of the unauthorized use.

Subparagraph six, action for injunction or damages, states that if an
individual's right of publicity is used within this state for advertis-
ing purposes, or for the purposes of trade without written consent the
individual is entitled to maintain an equitable action for violation of
the individual's right of privacy or right of publicity. In addition,
'to prevent and restrain the use thereof; an individual may also sue and
recover damages for any injuries sustained, including an amount equal to
the greater of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or compensatory
damages by reason of such use and if the defendant shall have knowingly
used such person's right of publicity the finder of fact, in its
discretion, may award exemplary damages.

Subparagraph seven clarifies that when using more than one person's
persona it is still a violation under the right of privacy or the right
of publicity if the necessary written permission is not obtained prior
to such use.


Subparagraphs eight, nine, ten and eleven are updated and modernized and
made easier to understand.

Subparagraph twelve discusses the termination of the post mortem right
of publicity.

Subparagraph thirteen discusses the statute of limitations which is one
year.

Section five amends the civil practice law and rules. Section six is the
severability clause.

Section seven is the effective date, on the one hundred and eightieth
day after becoming a law.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The term "Right of Publicity" originated in the United States Court of
Appeals for the Second Circuit in 1953 in Haelan Laboratories v.  Topps
Chewing Gum to describe the right of individuals to control the use of
their name and likenesses for commercial and other valuable purposes.
Since then, more than half of the states have granted rights of public-
ity to individuals through either the common law or by statute.

The Right of Publicity refers to every individual's inherent right to
control the commercial use of his or her personal characteristics, which
can include name, portrait or picture, voice or signature, each a part
of an individual's persona. Recently, in Lohann v. Take Two (Lohan v
Take-Two Interactive Software, Inc. 2018 NY Slip Op 02208 Decided on
March 29, 2018 Court of Appeals Fahey, J. Published by New York State
Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431.), the Court stated
that "A computer generated image may constitute a "portrait" within the
meaning of N.Y. Civ. Rights Law 50 and 51, but the disputed images in
the video game central to this matter were not recognizable as Lindsay
Lohan, and therefore, Lohan's complaint was properly dismissed."

The most critical function of the Right of Publicity is control. The
Right of Publicity, even though it is a property right, is not merely a
property asset, like a painting or real estate, for estate tax purposes.
The Right of Publicity ensures that if a person, or that person's
successor in interest, does not seek to commercialize the right, they
are not compelled to do so.

This bill provides for a post mortem right of publicity for forty years
after the death of an individual, allowing successors in interest to
provide notice of such interest through a public registration and post-
ing maintained by the New York Secretary of State. Along with providing
for a post mortem right of publicity the bill also has exclusions
consistent with constitutionally protected freedom of speech.

Finally, the Right of Publicity created through this legislation applies
to acts that occur within New York State.

In conclusion, this bill is balanced in protecting essential first
amendment rights consistent with current law while maintaining the
current status of the right of privacy law and still providing
protections for an individual's right of publicity, whether they are a
child or an adult, during life and for forty years after death.
 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2017 - died on 3rd Rdg. in both Houses.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take place on the one hundred and eightieth day after it
shall have become a law, and shall apply to all living individuals and
deceased individuals who died on or after such date.

summary: Establishes the right of privacy and the right of publicity for both living and deceased individuals; provides that an individual's persona is the personal property of the individual and is freely transferable and descendible; provides for the registration with the department of state of such rights of a deceased individual; and that the use of a digital replica for  purposes of trade within an expressive work shall be a violation.
title: Establishes the right of privacy and the right of publicity for both living and deceased individuals
